steps.title: A Namespace for the lab
steps.what: It creates the hello Namespace. Every other object in the file lives in it.
steps.why: It keeps the lab apart from anything else on your cluster. One delete would remove the whole app.

steps.title: Settings in a ConfigMap
steps.what: It holds the page message and the web server's settings file.
steps.why: Lab step 7 changes the message without rebuilding the image. Pods read it again when they restart.

steps.title: A login in a Secret
steps.what: It holds the login file the web server checks. Sign in as learner with the password kubernetes.
steps.why: Passwords belong in a Secret, apart from normal settings. You can then limit who reads them.

steps.title: The Deployment runs the web server
steps.what: It keeps two copies of the web server running. Each copy reads its message from the ConfigMap and its login from the Secret.
steps.why: With two copies, you can delete one Pod and still open the app. Lab step 6 shows this.

steps.title: One address for both Pods
steps.what: It gives the two Pods one stable name and port, 80, inside the cluster.
steps.why: Pods come and go with new addresses. In lab step 4, kubectl port-forward reaches the app through this Service.

notes.metadata.namespace: The Namespace this object lives in. Every lab object uses hello.
notes.ConfigMap:data.MESSAGE: The page message. The Deployment passes it to the web server as the MESSAGE environment variable.
notes.ConfigMap:data.default.conf.template: The web server's settings file. When the container starts, nginx fills in ${MESSAGE} from the environment.
notes.Secret:stringData.htpasswd: The login file the web server checks. It holds the user learner and a hashed password, not the plain one.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.spec.securityCo: Security settings for every container in the Pod.
Kubernetes refuses to start a container that would run as root. This image runs as user 101.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.spec.containers: Takes the variable's value from one key of a ConfigMap.
The container can read the login file but cannot change it.
Picks which ConfigMap keys become files. Only the settings template is mounted.
The ConfigMap key to turn into a file.
The file's name inside the mount folder.
Mounts a Secret as files. Each key becomes one file.
notes.Deployment:spec.selector.matchLabels.app: Match Pods whose app label is hello.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.metadata.labels: Every Pod gets the label app: hello, so the selector and the Service find it.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.spec.containers: The image to run: nginx's web server for non-root users, pinned by tag and digest.
The variable's name inside the container: MESSAGE.
CPU the container needs. 1000m equals one CPU, so 50m is a twentieth.
The page to ask for: /healthz, which answers without a login.
The port the web server listens on: 8080.
notes.Service:spec.selector.app: Send traffic to Pods labelled app: hello, the Pods from the Deployment above.
notes.Service:spec.ports[].targetPort: The port on the Pods where the Service forwards each request. The web server listens on 8080.

questions.question: How many copies of the web server does the Deployment keep running?
questions.explain: replicas: 2 asks for two Pods. Lab step 5 changes it to three.

questions.question: Where does the page message come from?
answers: The MESSAGE key in the hello-page ConfigMap
questions.explain: configMapKeyRef reads MESSAGE from hello-page. That is why lab step 7 changes the ConfigMap, not the image.

questions.question: Which port does the Service send traffic to on each Pod?
questions.explain: targetPort: 8080 is where the web server listens. Port 80 is the Service's own port.
